approaches.name: Build the n × m result
approaches.idea: Every element moves from `(i, j)` to `(j, i)`. Because the shape changes for non-square matrices, write into a new `n × m` matrix.
steps: Create `result` with `n` rows and `m` columns.
For every cell, set `result[j][i] = matrix[i][j]`.
Return `result`.
approaches.why: Every element must be read and written once, so O(m·n) is the lower bound; the new matrix is the required output, not extra working space. (Only a square matrix could be transposed in place, by swapping across the diagonal.)

spiral-matrix.pattern: Layer-by-layer traversal with four shrinking boundaries

approaches.name: Walk with a direction and a visited grid
approaches.idea: Simulate the walk: keep moving in the current direction (right, down, left, up) and turn clockwise whenever the next cell is outside the matrix or already visited.
steps: Keep a `visited` grid and direction vectors `dr = [0,1,0,−1]`, `dc = [1,0,−1,0]`.
Repeat m·n times: record the cell, mark it visited, and look at the next cell in the current direction.
If that cell is out of bounds or visited, turn clockwise; then step.
approaches.why: Each cell is visited once, but the visited grid costs as much memory as the matrix.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        dirs = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
        visited = [[False] * n for _ in range(m)]
        result, r, c, d = [], 0, 0, 0
        for _ in range(m * n):
            result.append(matrix[r][c])
            visited[r][c] = True
            nr, nc = r + dirs[d][0], c + dirs[d][1]
            if not (0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n) or visited[nr][nc]:
                d = (d + 1) % 4
                nr, nc = r + dirs[d][0], c + dirs[d][1]
            r, c = nr, nc
        return result

approaches.name: Four boundaries
approaches.idea: Keep `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`. Read the top row, the right column, the bottom row (reversed) and the left column (upwards), shrinking the matching boundary after each side.
steps: While `top ≤ bottom` and `left ≤ right`:
Read `top` row from `left` to `right`, then `top++`; read `right` column from `top` to `bottom`, then `right--`.
If `top ≤ bottom`: read `bottom` row from `right` to `left`, then `bottom--`.
If `left ≤ right`: read `left` column from `bottom` to `top`, then `left++`.
approaches.why: Each cell is read once and only four integers are kept (the output list is not extra space). The two `if` checks stop a single remaining row or column from being read twice.

spiral-matrix-ii.pattern: Spiral fill with four shrinking boundaries

approaches.name: Walk and turn when blocked
approaches.idea: Walk from the top-left placing 1, 2, 3, …; turn clockwise whenever the next cell is outside the grid or already filled (non-zero).
steps: Start with an all-zero n × n grid at `(0, 0)` heading right.
For `v` from 1 to n²: write `v`, then look at the next cell; if it is out of bounds or non-zero, turn clockwise; step.
approaches.why: Each cell is filled once. The grid itself acts as the visited marker, so no extra memory beyond the output is needed.

approaches.name: Fill layer by layer with four boundaries
approaches.idea: Fill the top row, right column, bottom row and left column of the current layer, shrinking each boundary as it is completed.
steps: `top = left = 0`, `bottom = right = n − 1`, `v = 1`.
While `v ≤ n²`: fill top row left→right (`top++`), right column top→bottom (`right--`), bottom row right→left (`bottom--`), left column bottom→top (`left++`).
Return the grid.
approaches.why: Each cell is written once with no per-step bounds checks. For a square grid the loop conditions alone stop at the centre.

rotate-image.pattern: Rotation = transpose + reverse rows, or four-way cyclic swaps per layer

approaches.name: Rotate into a copy, then copy back
approaches.idea: After a clockwise rotation, the new `(i, j)` holds the old `(n − 1 − j, i)`. Fill a second matrix that way and copy it back.
steps: Create `copy[i][j] = matrix[n − 1 − j][i]` for every cell.
Copy `copy` back into `matrix`.
approaches.why: Simple and correct, but it allocates a whole second matrix, which the problem forbids.

approaches.name: Transpose, then reverse each row
approaches.idea: Transposing sends `(i, j)` to `(j, i)`; reversing each row then sends it to `(j, n − 1 − i)` — exactly a 90° clockwise rotation. Both steps are in-place swaps.
steps: Transpose: for `i < j`, swap `matrix[i][j]` and `matrix[j][i]`.
Reverse every row.
approaches.why: Two passes of swaps, no extra matrix. Easy to remember and hard to get wrong in an interview.

approaches.name: Four-way cycle per layer
approaches.idea: Each element belongs to a cycle of four positions that rotate into each other: top → right → bottom → left. Rotate each cycle with one temporary value, layer by layer.
steps: For each layer `i < n/2`, for `j` from `i` to `n − 2 − i`:
approaches.why: Every element is moved exactly once (instead of twice in transpose + reverse), with one temporary variable.

set-matrix-zeroes.pattern: Use the first row and column as in-place marker arrays

approaches.name: Copy, then zero rows and columns from the copy
approaches.idea: Zeroing while scanning would spread new zeros. So read the zeros from an untouched copy and, for each one, clear its row and column in the original.
steps: Copy the matrix.
For every cell that is 0 in the copy, set its whole row and column to 0 in `matrix`.
approaches.why: Each zero clears up to m + n cells, and the copy doubles the memory.

approaches.name: Row and column flags
approaches.idea: Only which rows and which columns contain a zero matters. Record them in two boolean arrays, then clear in a second pass.
steps: Pass 1: for each zero at `(i, j)`, set `zeroRow[i]` and `zeroCol[j]`.
Pass 2: set `matrix[i][j] = 0` when `zeroRow[i]` or `zeroCol[j]`.

approaches.name: First row and column as the flags
approaches.idea: Store the row flags in column 0 and the column flags in row 0 of the matrix itself. Two extra booleans remember whether row 0 and column 0 themselves need clearing.
steps: Record `firstRowZero` / `firstColZero` = whether row 0 / column 0 contains a 0.
For `i, j ≥ 1`: if `matrix[i][j] == 0`, set `matrix[i][0] = 0` and `matrix[0][j] = 0`.
For `i, j ≥ 1`: zero the cell if `matrix[i][0] == 0` or `matrix[0][j] == 0`.
Finally clear row 0 and/or column 0 according to the two booleans.
approaches.why: Same two passes, but the markers live inside the matrix. Row 0 and column 0 are cleared last so their markers are read before being overwritten.

game-of-life.pattern: Simultaneous update via state encoding: keep the old state in bit 0, the new one in bit 1

approaches.name: Read from a copy
approaches.idea: All cells must update at once, so count neighbours on an unchanged copy of the board and write the new states into the original.
steps: Copy the board.
For each cell, count live neighbours among its 8 surrounding cells in the copy.
Apply the rules: alive next turn if `live == 3`, or if `live == 2` and the cell is alive now.
approaches.why: 8 neighbours per cell, plus a full copy of the board.

approaches.name: Encode the next state in bit 1
approaches.idea: Each cell only uses bit 0 (alive now). Write the next state into bit 1 while still reading neighbours through `& 1`, then shift every cell right by one.
steps: For each cell, count live neighbours using `board[r][c] & 1`.
If it lives next turn (`live == 3`, or `live == 2` and alive now), set `board[i][j] |= 2`.
Second pass: `board[i][j] >>= 1`.
approaches.why: Same neighbour counting, but the old state is never lost, so no copy is needed.

search-a-2d-matrix-ii.pattern: Staircase search from a corner where one move discards a whole row or column

approaches.name: Scan every cell
approaches.idea: Check every element against the target.
steps: Loop over all rows and columns.
Return true on a match, false after the scan.

approaches.name: Binary search each row
approaches.idea: Every row is sorted, so binary search each one. (Columns being sorted is not used.)
steps: For each row, binary search for `target`.
Return true if any search finds it.
approaches.why: m binary searches of length n.

approaches.name: Staircase from the top-right corner
approaches.idea: At the top-right cell, everything to the left is smaller and everything below is larger. If the cell is too big, its whole column is too big — move left. If too small, its whole row is too small — move down.
steps: Start at `r = 0`, `c = n − 1`.
While inside the matrix: equal → true; greater than target → `c--`; less → `r++`.
Return false when you walk off the matrix.
approaches.why: Each step removes one row or one column, so at most m + n steps. (The bottom-left corner works the same way.)

diagonal-traverse.pattern: Diagonals share i + j; alternate direction by parity and bounce off the edges

approaches.name: Scan the whole matrix for each diagonal
approaches.idea: For each diagonal index `d = i + j` from 0 to m + n − 2, scan every cell and collect those with `i + j == d` — rows bottom-to-top for even `d`, top-to-bottom for odd `d`.
steps: For `d` from 0 to m + n − 2:
If `d` is even, scan rows from m − 1 down to 0; otherwise from 0 up to m − 1.
Within the row, take the cell with `j = d − i` if it exists.
approaches.why: Every diagonal looks at all m rows, so most of the work finds nothing.

approaches.name: Group by i + j, reverse the even groups
approaches.idea: Bucket every cell by its diagonal `i + j` (scanning rows top to bottom), then output the buckets in order, reversing the even ones so they read upwards.
steps: Create m + n − 1 lists; append `mat[i][j]` to list `i + j` in row-major order.
For each `d`: append list `d` reversed if `d` is even, as-is if odd.
approaches.why: Each cell is touched twice, but the buckets hold a full copy of the matrix.

approaches.name: Walk the zig-zag and bounce off the edges
approaches.idea: Move up-right on even diagonals and down-left on odd ones. When a move would leave the matrix, step to the start of the next diagonal instead — which edge you hit decides whether that is right or down.
steps: Start at `(0, 0)`; repeat m·n times, recording the current cell.
Going up (`(r + c)` even): if at the last column, `r++`; else if at the top row, `c++`; else `r--, c++`.
Going down (odd): if at the last row, `c++`; else if at the first column, `r++`; else `r++, c--`.
approaches.why: One step per cell and no buffers besides the output. The last-column / last-row checks come first so corners turn the right way.
